keep: The asp is Octavian's picture of her death, carried in his triumph. Plutarch, who passed it on, wrote that nobody knew how she died.
lede: The Greek who left the fullest account of her said her beauty was not altogether incomparable. What held people was her talk. The asp, he admitted, nobody could vouch for.
copy: Cleopatra VII was the last of the Ptolemies, a Macedonian family that had ruled Egypt for generations without learning its language. Plutarch, whose Life of Antony is the fullest ancient account of her, says the kings of Egypt before her had not even made an effort to learn the native tongue, and some had given up their Macedonian. She answered most foreign envoys herself. He names Ethiopians, Troglodytes, Hebrews, Arabians, Syrians, Medes and Parthians, and says she knew the speech of many other peoples. That is seven, named. The nine languages of the modern books are somebody's arithmetic, not his.

Her power was money and ships. When Antony gathered his fleet at Ephesus for the war with Octavian, Plutarch counts eight hundred warships, and Cleopatra furnished two hundred of them. She added twenty thousand talents and supplies for the whole army. Antony's friends wanted her sent home to Egypt; she persuaded his general to let her stay. The famous first meeting with Caesar, rolled in a carpet, is a bed-sack in Plutarch's Life of Caesar, tied with a cord and carried in by Apollodorus the Sicilian. After Actium, Octavian wanted her alive. She would, Plutarch says, add greatly to the glory of his triumph.

How she died is the part nobody knew. Plutarch gives an asp hidden under figs, then an asp kept in a water jar, then poison carried in a hollow comb in her hair, and says 'the truth of the matter no one knows'. No snake was seen in the room. Some said her arm showed two faint punctures. Cassius Dio found only slight pricks on the arm. She was thirty-nine, by Plutarch's count, and had shared power with Antony for more than fourteen years. Octavian had an image of her with the asp clinging to her carried in his triumph. That is the picture that lasted.

bio.why: A Pulitzer-winning biographer reading against hostile ancient sources to reconstruct a shrewd, capable ruler. Read Plutarch's Life of Antony beside it; it is free, it is short, and it is where nearly every story about her starts. This house has read Plutarch and Dio, not Schiff.

contested: The witness is lost. Plutarch names one source from inside the room: her physician Olympus, who, Plutarch says, helped her plan her death and published a history of it. That book does not survive. Everything that does was written under the empire of the man who beat her, and the two main accounts disagree on detail. Plutarch has two slight and indistinct punctures and says Octavian seems to have believed in the asp; Dio has slight pricks and gives the asp as one story among others, beside a poisoned hairpin. Neither writer claims to know. The modern argument over whether to read her as a seducer or a head of state runs on these same few pages, and nothing new is likely to settle it.
